title: Strong coupling of a reconfigurable ${}^{171}$Yb atom array to a tunable telecom-band nanofiber cavity
authors: Hideki Ozawa, Neville Chen, Yusuke Hisai, Shunichiro Hashimoto, Kenichi N. Komagata, Remi T. Oddon, Shanjou Yang, Seitaro Horikawa, Seigo Kikura, Shigehito Miki, Takao Aoki, Tadayuki Yoshitake, Hideki Konishi, Shinichi Sunami, Akihisa Goban, Ryotaro Inoue
abstract: Nanophotonic cavities provide strong atom-photon coupling in a compact, directly fiber-coupled geometry, while a reconfigurable array of $^{171}$Yb atoms combines high-fidelity gates with a metastable qubit state coupled directly to a telecom-band transition, making the two a natural interface between neutral-atom quantum processors and telecom quantum networks. Here, we realize strong atom-cavity coupling on the ${}^{3}\mathrm{P}_0 \leftrightarrow {}^{3}\mathrm{D}_1$ transition of ${}^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$, establishing, to our knowledge, the first neutral-atom cavity-QED system to reach the single-atom strong-coupling regime on a telecom-band atomic transition. Reflection spectroscopy of a single-sided cavity yields a single-atom internal cooperativity of $C_{\mathrm{in}}=5.6(1.0)$ and collective coupling following $\sqrt{N}$ scaling up to $N=5$ atoms, with homogeneous coupling at antinodes over $\sim$200 $\mathrmμ$m along the nanofiber. Thermal tuning of a fiber Bragg grating provides in situ control of the cavity outcoupling rate over two orders of magnitude from the undercoupled to the overcoupled regime, relevant for various atom-cavity protocols. We confirm compatibility with reconfigurable atom arrays by demonstrating 99.95(6)\% imaging fidelity and trap lifetimes comparable to free-space array, at 1 $\mathrmμ$m from the nanofiber axis. Moreover, the diameter-engineered antireflection design of the nanofiber enables tweezer-based atom transport across the nanofiber with no measurable loss or heating at 4.5 $\mathrmμ$m above the nanofiber, supporting a two-layer architecture for the nanofiber-integrated atom array. From the demonstrated atom-cavity coupling, atom capacity, and cavity mode profile, we project time-multiplexed remote atom-atom entanglement generation at 40 kHz, with prospects for further scaling through technical enhancements and channel multiplexing.
summary: The research demonstrates strong coupling between a reconfigurable array of ${}^{171}	ext{Yb}$ atoms and a tunable nanofiber cavity operating at telecom wavelengths. By characterizing the coupling strength and the tunability of the cavity, the authors establish a robust interface for quantum networking. This paves the way for high-rate, multiplexed entanglement generation necessary for distributed quantum computing.
main_problem: The goal is to create a high-rate, high-fidelity quantum interconnect by coupling a reconfigurable array of ${}^{171}	ext{Yb}$ atoms to a tunable telecom-band nanofiber cavity.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated strong atom-photon coupling on the telecom-band transition, achieving single-atom cooperativity of $C_{	ext{in}}=5.6$ and projecting a time-multiplexed entanglement generation rate of $40 	ext{ kHz}$.
method: The study uses reflection spectroscopy on a single-sided cavity, combined with optical tweezer trapping and transport, to characterize the atom-cavity interaction.
model_or_system: The platform combines a nanofiber cavity (formed by two FBGs) operating at $1389 	ext{ nm}$ with an array of ${}^{171}	ext{Yb}$ atoms trapped in optical tweezers. The system is designed to interface neutral-atom quantum processors with telecom quantum networks.
key_observables: Single-atom internal cooperativity ($C_{	ext{in}}$), collective coupling scaling ($\sqrt{N}$), and the cavity outcoupling rate ($\kappa_{	ext{ex}}$).
important_parameters: Telecom wavelength ($1389 	ext{ nm}$), single-atom coupling ($g/2\pi \approx 1.86 	ext{ MHz}$), and the ability to tune $\kappa_{	ext{ex}}$ over two orders of magnitude.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on single-sided cavity input-output models and assumes compatibility between the tweezer trapping light and the cavity coupling mechanism.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the platform overview, the tweezer array setup, and SEM images of the fabricated nanofiber, supporting the characterization of coupling strength and transport feasibility.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical platform and coupling strength via spectroscopy, to demonstrating tunability of the cavity coupling rate, and finally to analyzing the compatibility for high-rate, multiplexed quantum networking protocols.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes cavity QED into the telecom regime using neutral atoms, which is a critical step for building scalable quantum networks and quantum repeaters.
